text:
**The engine inspection.** The FAA and the engine maker have told airlines to inspect a part on one engine type. Some of Kestrel's aircraft use it. A passenger's video of mechanics working on an engine at the gate is going round on TikTok.

Known: the inspections are a precaution and start this week; no Kestrel aircraft has had a problem with this part.
Not known: how many aircraft; how long each check takes; whether any part must be replaced.
reading: Precautionary engine inspections begin this week; they may cause delays or some cancellations. No Kestrel aircraft has a confirmed problem with the part.

text: The inspections found worn parts on three Kestrel aircraft. They will stay on the ground for about two weeks while new parts arrive. All other aircraft have been cleared to fly. Kestrel will have to cancel or merge some flights in the next two weeks, Thanksgiving week included.
reading: Worn parts on three Kestrel aircraft ground them for about two weeks. Cancellations or merged flights affect Thanksgiving week and may continue into week 5.

text:
**Government shutdown.** Overnight, Congress missed its funding deadline, and parts of the federal government shut down. Some federal workers have been sent home; others, such as air traffic controllers and TSA officers, must keep working without pay. Nobody knows how long it will last.

Known: Social Security payments and the Postal Service continue.
Not known: how long it will last; when federal workers will be paid; which services will slow down.

Air traffic controllers and TSA officers keep working, without pay. Some airports report longer security lines.
reading: A partial federal government shutdown has begun with air traffic controllers and TSA agents working without pay, causing longer security lines and operational delays primarily affecting Kestrel's main bases in Orlando and Philadelphia while travelers navigate the uncertainty.

text:
**Government shutdown — update.** The Senate passed a short-term funding bill; the House plans to vote after Christmas. Federal workers have been told they will get back pay once the government reopens. Their December 30 paycheck may be missed.

The FAA says it may slow traffic at busy airports if more controllers call in sick.
reading: As a potential funding gap threatens federal operations and air traffic controller absenteeism, passengers at Kestrel bases in Orlando and Philadelphia may face localized delays heading into the winter holidays.

text:
**Week 8, Tuesday, December 22 and Wednesday, December 23: a 48-hour strike by the ground handling contractor's workers in Orlando and Philadelphia.**
- Baggage handlers, cabin cleaners, wheelchair agents and fuelers employed by the contractor plan to walk out for 48 hours.
- The contractor says it will bring in replacement staff "where it can". Turnarounds will be slower; some flights may be late or canceled.
- The union says the strike "may be extended". Talks continue.
- It is the busiest holiday week of the year.
reading: Known 48-hour ground handling strike at both bases on December 22–23; replacement staffing may be incomplete and extension is possible.

text: **Known crisis outcome, week 9.** The ground handling strike lasted 48 hours and was not extended. The contractor covered about half of its shifts with replacement staff.
reading: A brief forty-eight-hour ground handling strike caused some flight cancellations at Kestrel Air bases as replacement staff covered only half of the required shifts, though operations are expected to normalize quickly.
